Neonates of the Lesser grass finch (Emberizoides ypiranganus) emerge at a modest body mass, reflecting the altricial condition typical of many Neotropical passerines. At hatching, which follows an incubation period largely dependent on ambient thermal conditions, newly hatched chicks exhibit a wet weight of just 1.9 grams [Wwb = 1.9 grams], a value consistent with the minimal provisioning of yolk reserves. The initial wet weight recorded shortly after laying is slightly higher, at 2.7 grams [Ww0 = 2.7 grams], suggesting a small degree of water loss during development. These measurements were derived from a series of captive-bred individuals housed under controlled environmental chambers set to a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Under these conditions, the age at hatching was determined to be 13.7 days [ab = 13.7 days], a duration typical for small-bodied finches and one that appears to be finely tuned to the prevailing nest temperature at a temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C]. Such precise developmental timing underscores the tight coupling between incubation microclimate and embryonic growth rates in this species.

The post-hatching developmental trajectory of the nestling period is characterized by rapid somatic growth as chicks transition from dependence on yolk sac reserves to receiving regular parental provisioning. A critical milestone in this phase is fledging, which under optimal thermal conditions occurs relatively early in the life cycle. When maintained at an ambient temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], young birds achieve their first flight at approximately 10 days after hatching [tx = approximately 10 days after hatching], a remarkably swift transition that likely reflects selective pressures to escape ground-level predation in the open grasslands this species inhabits. This rapid development is followed by a more gradual phase of physiological maturation. The attainment of sexual maturity, or puberty, is reached considerably later. Under the same thermal regime of 41.6 °C individuals become reproductively active at about 30 days after hatching [tp = about 30 days after hatching], a stage defined by the onset of gonadal development and the first appearance of adult plumage character at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]istics.

Reproductive scheduling in the Lesser grass finch is tightly constrained by both seasonal resource availability and the energetic demands of egg production. The time elapsed since birth until the first successful brood is a substantial period, measured at 365 days after hatching [tR = 365 days after hatching] under conditions held at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. This delay means that most individuals do not contribute to the breeding population until their second calendar year after fledging, a life-history strategy that may buffer against years of poor rainfall in the ephemeral wetlands of northern Argentina and Uruguay. Once reproductive activity commences, the potential reproductive output is modest but consistent. Females typically lay 2 to 3 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = 2 to 3 eggs per clutch], a fecundity value that is near the median for emberizine finches. The frequency of nesting attempts, however, can be high if conditions permit, with available data suggesting that individuals may produce approximately 1 to 2 clutches each year [F_R_i = approximately 1 to 2 clutches each year] when environmental conditions are favorable.

Adult body size in Emberizoides ypiranganus is relatively small compared to other members of the Thraupidae, with a notably modest ultimate wet weight. The maximum adult body mass recorded for the species, based on a large sample of museum specimens and captive-raised individuals, is 20.17 grams [Wwi = 20.17 grams]. This figure represents the asymptotic mass that individuals attain after the completion of structural growth and the accumulation of adequate fat reserves for the non-breeding season. In contrast, the initial wet weight of a newly laid egg, measured before any significant embryonic development, is approximately 2.7 grams [Ww0 = approximately 2.7 grams], a value that represents a substantial parental investment relative to adult body size. The ratio of neonatal mass to adult mass in this species, approximately 9.4 percent, is characteristic of altricial songbirds that must rely entirely on parental care for the initial weeks of life. These measurements were compiled from longitudinal growth studies conducted at two separate field stations in the Pampas region.

Longevity data for the Lesser grass finch remain sparse, but the available records from both wild populations and captive colonies indicate a maximum lifespan that is moderate for a passerine of its dimensions. The oldest documented individual reached an age of 10 years [am = 10 years] under controlled conditions maintained at 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C], a figure that aligns with the upper range of survival reported for other small-bodied grassland finches from the Southern Cone. This extended lifespan is notable given the species' relatively rapid pace of early development, particularly the achievement of first flight at just 10 days after hatching [tx = 10 days after hatching] recorded at the same thermal regime at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C]. It suggests a life-history strategy that trades a small initial body size and high early mortality against the potential for multiple reproductive seasons over a decade of adult life. Puberty is achieved swiftly at one month after hatching (30 days after hatching) [tp = 30 days after hatching], while first reproduction is deferred until nearly a full year after hatching (365 days after hatching) [tR = 365 days after hatching], implying a period of social or territory acquisition that precedes actual breeding, a phenomenon common in many Neotropical finches at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C] at a temperature of 41.6 °C [T = 41.6 °C].
